name: Andorra
description:
Andorra has moved to position itself as a digital-asset hub, approving a dedicated law in 2022 that sets rules for crypto service providers under the Andorran Financial Authority. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro is used.

The principality's low-tax regime and mountain setting have attracted crypto businesses and residents, with gains generally taxed at low rates as part of income. Providers must meet anti-money-laundering standards.

Andorra la Vella hosts a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Andorran places where you can spend sats.

name: United Arab Emirates
description:
The United Arab Emirates has become a magnet for Bitcoin businesses and talent, with purpose-built free zones and regulators such as Dubai's VARA and Abu Dhabi's ADGM. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the dirham remains the official currency.

There is no personal income tax and no capital gains tax for individuals, which has drawn companies and high earners; the federal government has also introduced a payment-token framework and the Central Bank supervises stablecoins. The country hosts Bitcoin MENA, a major regional Bitcoin-only conference.

From Dubai to Abu Dhabi and Ras Al Khaimah, meetups and bitcoin-accepting venues keep the scene busy. Use this map to find the Emirati places where you can spend sats.

name: Antigua and Barbuda
description:
Antigua and Barbuda is a small twin-island nation with an offshore-finance base, where Bitcoin remains a niche interest. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the East Caribbean dollar is the official currency.

Authorities have shown some openness to digital-asset business while tightening anti-money-laundering oversight, but there is no broad bitcoin licensing regime. Local adoption is minimal.

Saint John's hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Antiguan places where you can spend sats.

name: Anguilla
description:
Anguilla, a British Overseas Territory, has experimented with digital-asset legislation, passing a utility-token framework in 2020. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the East Caribbean dollar is the official currency.

The financial regulator has taken a light-touch approach, and there is no broad bitcoin licensing regime, so adoption remains small and mostly peer-to-peer.

The Valley hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Anguillan places where you can spend sats.

name: Armenia
description:
Armenia has a strong tech and engineering base, and Bitcoin has found a small but growing following in Yerevan and beyond. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the dram remains the official currency.

The central bank has cautioned that crypto is not recognised or regulated, and there is no dedicated licensing framework, so adoption remains mostly peer-to-peer.

Yerevan hosts a small but engaged Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Armenian places where you can spend sats.

name: Angola
description:
Angola has taken a hard line on crypto: in 2024 its parliament approved a law banning cryptocurrency mining and restricting trading, citing electricity theft and money-laundering risks. The kwanza is the only legal tender.

The central bank has warned against virtual assets for years, and the new law adds criminal penalties for unlicensed mining. Despite the restrictions, interest persists among a young population facing a weak kwanza.

Luanda hosts a small, cautious Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Angolan places where you can spend sats.

name: Argentina
description:
Argentina has emerged as one of the world's most active Bitcoin economies, a response to decades of high inflation and strict currency controls that make saving in pesos difficult. Bitcoin is not legal tender here, but it is legal to hold, trade and mine, and it has become a popular store of value and a channel for remittances.

The country has a deep grassroots culture: LaBitconf, first held in Buenos Aires in 2013, is among the oldest Bitcoin conferences in Latin America, and a network of meetups and NGOs such as Bitcoin Argentina keeps the community growing. Peer-to-peer trading volumes and wallets like Lemon and Belo have made sats part of everyday life.

President Javier Milei, elected in 2023 on a libertarian platform, has been openly pro-Bitcoin and favors currency competition, though the peso remains legal tender. Use this map to find the growing number of Argentine places where you can spend sats.

name: Austria
description:
Austria has a long-standing Bitcoin community, with Vienna's early meetups and the Bitcoin Austria association helping put the country on the map. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

Since 2022, capital gains on bitcoin have been taxed at a flat 27.5%, a rate shared with other capital income, and losses can be offset. Service providers must register with the financial authorities for anti-money-laundering supervision.

From Vienna to Graz, Linz and Salzburg, meetups and bitcoin-accepting businesses keep the scene growing. Use this map to find the Austrian places where you can spend sats.

name: Australia
description:
Australia was an early mover on Bitcoin policy, scrapping double taxation in 2017 by removing GST from bitcoin purchases and treating it more like money. Bitcoin is legal, though not legal tender, and exchanges have had to register with AUSTRAC since 2018.

For tax, the ATO treats bitcoin as a capital gains asset: individuals who hold for more than a year can qualify for a 50% CGT discount, while mining and trading income is taxed differently. Home-grown exchanges such as CoinJar, founded in 2013, and BTC Markets serve a mature local market.

From Sydney and Melbourne to Brisbane and Perth, meetups and bitcoin-accepting merchants keep the scene active. Use this map to find the Australian places where you can spend sats.

name: Aruba
description:
Aruba, a Caribbean constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, has a tourism-driven economy and a small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Aruban florin remains the official currency.

The central bank has taken a cautious line on crypto, and there is no dedicated licensing framework, so adoption remains minimal and peer-to-peer.

Oranjestad hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Aruban places where you can spend sats.

name: Aland
description:
Åland, an autonomous, demilitarised region of Finland, uses the euro and has a very small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

Finnish and EU rules apply, and there is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

Mariehamn hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Åland places where you can spend sats.

name: Azerbaijan
description:
Azerbaijan has a young, connected population and a growing curiosity about Bitcoin, though the central bank has not recognised it as legal tender. The manat remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned against crypto, and there is no dedicated licensing framework, so activity is mostly peer-to-peer and informal.

Baku hosts a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Azerbaijani places where you can spend sats.

name: Barbados
description:
Barbados has been among the more fintech-friendly Caribbean nations, and Bitcoin has a small but engaged following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Barbadian dollar is pegged to the US dollar.

There is no capital gains tax, and the financial regulator has studied a framework for digital assets, though no broad licensing regime is in force. Adoption remains niche and peer-to-peer.

Bridgetown hosts a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Barbadian places where you can spend sats.

name: Bangladesh
description:
Bangladesh is one of South Asia's largest grassroots crypto markets, but the authorities have taken a hard line: the central bank warned in 2017 that virtual-currency transactions are illegal and punishable under foreign-exchange law. The taka is the only legal tender.

Despite the ban, peer-to-peer trading and community interest have persisted, helped by a huge remittance economy and a young population. Policymakers have periodically discussed a legal framework, but none has been adopted.

Dhaka and Chittagong host a quiet but persistent Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Bangladeshi places where you can spend sats.

name: Bulgaria
description:
Bulgaria made headlines in 2017 when authorities seized roughly 200,000 bitcoins from an organised-crime network—one of the largest government bitcoin hauls ever. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

The country applies a flat 10% income tax, and crypto gains are taxed at that rate, making it one of the lighter regimes in the EU. Providers are supervised under anti-money-laundering rules and, increasingly, EU-wide MiCA.

Sofia and Plovdiv host meetups and a small but active Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Bulgarian places where you can spend sats.

name: Bahrain
description:
Bahrain was one of the first Gulf states to regulate crypto, issuing a dedicated crypto-asset rulebook through its central bank in 2019. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Bahraini dinar remains the official currency.

The framework allows licensed exchanges and brokers to operate, and Bahrain has attracted regional firms such as CoinMENA and a Binance entity. There is no personal income tax, which adds to its appeal.

Manama hosts a small but active Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Bahraini places where you can spend sats.

name: Saint Barthelemy
description:
Saint Barthélemy, a French overseas collectivity in the Caribbean, uses the euro and has a very small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

French and EU rules apply, and there is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

Gustavia hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the places where you can spend sats.

name: Bermuda
description:
Bermuda was an early mover on digital-asset regulation, passing the Digital Asset Business Act in 2018 and creating one of the world's first comprehensive licensing regimes under its monetary authority. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Bermudian dollar is pegged to the US dollar.

The island's reinsurance and offshore-finance pedigree, plus no income or capital gains tax, has attracted crypto firms and conferences. Regulation remains among the most developed in the Caribbean.

Hamilton hosts a small but international Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Bermudian places where you can spend sats.

name: Brunei
description:
Brunei has kept Bitcoin at arm's length: the central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised as legal tender, and no licensing framework exists for digital-asset businesses. The Brunei dollar remains the official currency.

Interest remains small and informal, with activity largely peer-to-peer. The country's tight financial rules and Sharia-compliant finance framework leave little room for unlicensed crypto services.

Bandar Seri Begawan hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Bruneian places where you can spend sats.

name: Bolivia
description:
Bolivia reversed course on Bitcoin in 2024, when the central bank lifted a ban on crypto transactions and allowed regulated electronic payment channels to handle virtual assets. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the boliviano remains the official currency.

The change came as dollar shortages and economic pressure pushed more Bolivians toward digital alternatives, and peer-to-peer trading has risen sharply. Tax and anti-money-laundering rules are still being defined.

La Paz and Santa Cruz host small but growing Bitcoin communities. Use this map to find the Bolivian places where you can spend sats.

name: Brazil
description:
Brazil is Latin America's largest Bitcoin market and home to its first bitcoin ETF, launched in 2021. Bitcoin is legal, though not legal tender, and since 2022 it has been recognised as a virtual asset under a national framework that puts the central bank in charge of licensing service providers.

The use cases are strong in a country with a large unbanked population and expensive remittances: peer-to-peer trading and exchanges are widely used, and some municipal governments, including Rio de Janeiro, have explored accepting bitcoin for taxes and holding it in public reserves.

From São Paulo to Rio and Florianópolis, meetups and bitcoin-accepting merchants keep the scene growing. Use this map to find the Brazilian places where you can spend sats.

name: The Bahamas
description:
The Bahamas was an early mover on crypto regulation, passing the Digital Assets and Registered Exchanges (DARE) Act in 2020 under the Securities Commission. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Bahamian dollar is pegged one-to-one to the US dollar.

The collapse of FTX—which was headquartered in Nassau—in 2022 led the country to strengthen the DARE framework in 2024. The Bahamas levies no personal income tax and no capital gains tax.

Nassau hosts a small but internationally minded Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Bahamian places where you can spend sats.

name: Bhutan
description:
Bhutan has quietly become one of the world's most surprising bitcoin holders, mining with abundant hydropower through its state investment arm, Druk Holding & Investments, since around 2019. Bitcoin is not legal tender, and the ngultrum remains the official currency.

On-chain researchers have identified wallets linked to Bhutan holding thousands of bitcoin, making the kingdom—by some measures—one of the largest known state-level holders. The mining runs largely on clean hydroelectricity.

Thimphu hosts a small, developing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Bhutanese places where you can spend sats.

name: Botswana
description:
Botswana has a small but growing Bitcoin community, underpinned by one of Africa's more stable economies and high mobile-money use. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the pula remains the official currency.

The central bank and the non-bank regulator have warned that crypto is not legal tender and carries risk, and the country has been working on a framework to supervise service providers. Adoption remains modest and peer-to-peer.

Gaborone and Francistown host occasional meetups. Use this map to find the Botswana places where you can spend sats.

name: Canada
description:
Canada has a habit of firsts in Bitcoin: the world's first Bitcoin ATM opened in a Vancouver coffee shop in 2013, and in 2021 the Purpose Bitcoin ETF became the first spot bitcoin ETF to trade anywhere. Bitcoin is legal here, though not legal tender.

Exchanges and brokers must register with FINTRAC as money services businesses, and bitcoin is generally treated as a commodity for tax purposes, with gains taxed as capital gains or income. Cheap hydro power in provinces such as Quebec and Alberta has also drawn bitcoin miners.

From Toronto and Vancouver to Montreal, active meetups and merchants keep the community growing. Use this map to find the Canadian places where you can spend sats.

name: Switzerland
description:
Switzerland has positioned itself as one of Europe's most Bitcoin-friendly countries, with the canton of Zug hosting a dense cluster of Bitcoin companies and foundations. Since 2016 the city of Zug has even accepted bitcoin for municipal tax payments.

Rather than write bespoke rules, the Swiss financial regulator FINMA applies existing financial-market law to bitcoin businesses and issues guidance. Capital gains on bitcoin are generally tax-free at the federal level for private investors, though wealth and some cantonal taxes still apply.

Cities lead the way: Lugano's Plan B has turned the lakeside city into a Bitcoin hub that accepts BTC for taxes, parking and public services, while meetups and companies in Zurich and Zug keep the community connected. Use this map to find the Swiss places where you can spend sats.

name: Ivory Coast
description:
Ivory Coast is one of West Africa's biggest economies, with a fast-growing mobile-money market that has helped Bitcoin gain a foothold. Bitcoin is not legal tender, and the CFA franc remains the official currency.

The regional central bank, the BCEAO, has warned that crypto is not recognised, and there is no dedicated licensing regime yet. Adoption is grassroots, driven by remittances and a young population.

Abidjan hosts a small but active Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Ivorian places where you can spend sats.

name: Chile
description:
Chile has one of Latin America's more mature Bitcoin markets, home to exchanges such as Buda and CryptoMKT that were founded in the mid-2010s. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the peso remains the official currency.

A Fintech Law that took effect in 2024 brought crypto service providers under the financial regulator, the CMF, and requires them to register. The tax authority treats bitcoin as an asset: trading gains are taxed as income, while crypto sales are not subject to VAT.

Santiago and Valparaíso host meetups and a growing set of bitcoin-accepting businesses. Use this map to find the Chilean places where you can spend sats.

name: Cameroon
description:
Cameroon is one of Central Africa's most active crypto markets, with widespread mobile money and a young population driving adoption. Bitcoin is not legal tender, and the Central African CFA franc remains the official currency.

The regional central bank, the BEAC, has warned that crypto is not recognised and lacks a legal framework, while officials have studied how to regulate it. Adoption remains grassroots and largely peer-to-peer.

Douala and Yaoundé host a growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Cameroonian places where you can spend sats.

name: China
description:
China was once the centre of gravity for Bitcoin: it hosted most of the world's mining hashrate and its earliest exchanges. That changed in September 2021, when regulators declared all crypto-related activities illegal and mining was effectively banned, triggering a mass migration of miners abroad.

Holding bitcoin is not a criminal offence—courts have recognised it as property—but trading, exchanges and related services are prohibited, and the digital yuan is the state's official alternative. Enforcement varies, and peer-to-peer activity persists.

Despite the restrictions, a resilient developer and user community keeps Bitcoin alive, while Hong Kong operates under its own licensing regime. Use this map to find the places where you can spend sats.

name: Colombia
description:
Colombia is one of Latin America's fastest-growing Bitcoin markets, with remittances, inflation and a large population of unbanked users driving adoption. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the peso remains the official currency.

Regulation is still maturing: authorities have run a regulatory sandbox for exchanges and debated a dedicated crypto law, while the tax authority treats bitcoin as an asset subject to income or capital gains tax.

Bogotá and Medellín host some of the region's liveliest Bitcoin meetups, and merchants in both cities accept sats. Use this map to find the Colombian places where you can spend sats.

name: Costa Rica
description:
Costa Rica has one of Central America's more developed tech scenes and a growing Bitcoin community, concentrated in San José and the Pacific coast expat hubs. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the colón remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised and carries no consumer protection, and there is no dedicated licensing regime yet, so adoption is mostly peer-to-peer and merchant-driven.

San José and the coastal towns of Guanacaste host meetups and a scattering of bitcoin-accepting businesses. Use this map to find the Costa Rican places where you can spend sats.

name: Cuba
description:
Cuba has become an unlikely Bitcoin hotspot, as sanctions, limited banking access and expensive remittances push Cubans toward sats. Bitcoin is not legal tender, but the Central Bank recognised and began regulating virtual assets in 2021.

That recognition let licensed providers operate, and Bitcoin and the Lightning Network are widely used to receive money from abroad and to pay for everyday goods. The peso remains the official currency.

Havana's Bitcoin community, and users across the island, keep the scene growing despite connectivity challenges. Use this map to find the Cuban places where you can spend sats.

name: Curaçao
description:
Curaçao, a Caribbean constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, punches well above its weight in Bitcoin, with a dense network of accepting merchants for a small island. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Netherlands Antillean guilder is the currency.

Adoption grew organically around Willemstad and its tourism economy, even though the central bank has cautioned against crypto and there is no dedicated licensing framework.

Willemstad hosts an active Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Curaçao places where you can spend sats.

name: Czechia
description:
Czechia, and Prague in particular, has one of Europe's deepest Bitcoin cultures. The city is home to SatoshiLabs, the company behind the Trezor hardware wallet, and to Paralelní Polis, a Bitcoin-focused cafe and hackerspace founded in 2014.

Bitcoin is legal and increasingly mainstream: a growing number of shops, cafes and services accept it, and Prague hosts BTC Prague, one of the continent's largest Bitcoin-only conferences. Czech law treats bitcoin as an asset, and long-term private holdings enjoy capital gains relief.

From the Bitcoin cafes of Prague to local meetups around the country, the community is one of the most dedicated in Europe. Use this map to find the Czech places where you can spend sats.

name: Germany
description:
Germany was one of the first major economies to give bitcoin a legal home, when the Federal Ministry of Finance classified it as private money back in 2013. Bitcoin is not legal tender, but it is legal to buy, hold and spend, and it is exempt from VAT when used as payment.

The tax treatment is famously friendly: private investors who hold bitcoin for more than a year owe no capital gains tax on the sale, while shorter holdings are taxed as income. Regulated banks and custodians can offer bitcoin services, and Berlin's room77 pub has accepted bitcoin since the early days, making it one of the oldest bitcoin merchants anywhere.

From Berlin and Munich to the Ruhr, meetups and merchant adoption keep the scene active in Europe's largest economy. Use this map to find the German places where you can spend sats.

name: Denmark
description:
Denmark has a compact Bitcoin scene centred on Copenhagen, with regular meetups and a growing interest in self-custody. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Danish krone remains the official currency.

Tax is a moving target: gains are currently taxed as speculative income at ordinary rates, and the government has proposed a simpler 26% regime. Service providers must comply with anti-money-laundering rules.

Copenhagen's meetups and a small set of bitcoin-accepting businesses keep the community connected, with interest spreading to Aarhus and Odense. Use this map to find the Danish places where you can spend sats.

name: Dominica
description:
Dominica, a small Eastern Caribbean island nation, uses the East Caribbean dollar and has a very small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

The regional central bank has cautioned against crypto, and Dominica has no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

Roseau hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Dominica places where you can spend sats.

name: Dominican Republic
description:
The Dominican Republic is one of the Caribbean's largest economies and a major remittance recipient, and Bitcoin has gained a following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Dominican peso remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised or regulated, and a dedicated framework is still in development, so adoption is mostly peer-to-peer.

Santo Domingo and Punta Cana host a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Dominican places where you can spend sats.

name: Algeria
description:
Algeria has one of the strictest stances in the world: a 2018 finance law banned the purchase, sale and use of virtual currencies, and later rules extended the prohibition to mining and promotion. The Algerian dinar is the only legal tender.

Authorities cite currency controls and anti-money-laundering concerns, and enforcement has kept formal adoption minimal, though interest and small peer-to-peer flows persist. No licensing framework currently exists.

Algiers hosts a small, cautious Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Algerian places where you can spend sats.

name: Estonia
description:
Estonia earned a reputation as a digital trailblazer, and in 2017 it was among the first EU countries to license crypto service providers. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

After money-laundering scandals, Estonia tightened its rules sharply and revoked hundreds of licences, and providers are now supervised under EU-wide MiCA. Gains on bitcoin are taxed as capital income.

Tallinn's meetups and a tech-heavy community keep Bitcoin on the agenda in the Baltic. Use this map to find the Estonian places where you can spend sats.

name: Egypt
description:
Egypt is one of the Middle East and North Africa's biggest grassroots crypto markets, as repeated devaluations of the pound push users toward digital alternatives. Trading in bitcoin is largely prohibited under a 2020 banking law, and the Egyptian pound is the only legal tender.

The Central Bank of Egypt has warned against crypto and has not licensed any providers, though enforcement is uneven and peer-to-peer activity persists. Authorities have studied a digital pound and, at times, signalled openness to a regulated framework.

Cairo and Alexandria host a cautious but persistent Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Egyptian places where you can spend sats.

name: Spain
description:
Spain has become one of Europe's liveliest Bitcoin markets, with Madrid and Barcelona among the continent's leaders in bitcoin ATMs and a fast-growing merchant scene. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

The tax agency treats bitcoin as an asset: gains are taxed as savings income, and residents must declare holdings, including those held abroad under the Modelo 721 form. The CNMV and Bank of Spain supervise providers as EU-wide MiCA rules take hold.

From Madrid and Barcelona to Valencia and Seville, meetups and bitcoin-accepting businesses keep the community buzzing. Use this map to find the Spanish places where you can spend sats.

name: Ethiopia
description:
Ethiopia has emerged as an unexpected force in Bitcoin mining, with state-owned Ethiopian Electric Power signing deals to supply cheap hydroelectricity to miners and earn scarce foreign currency. Bitcoin is not legal tender, and the birr remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned against crypto and does not recognise it as legal tender, and no dedicated law governs the sector. The mining push, however, has put the country on the global hashrate map with abundant renewable power.

Addis Ababa hosts a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Ethiopian places where you can spend sats.

name: Finland
description:
Finland has a small but tech-savvy Bitcoin community, concentrated around Helsinki and its strong startup ecosystem. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

Finland was an early mover on regulation, requiring virtual-currency providers to register with the FIN-FSA back in 2019. Capital income from bitcoin is taxed at 30%, rising to 34% above 30,000 euros, with losses deductible.

Helsinki's meetups and a modest set of bitcoin-accepting businesses keep the scene going. Use this map to find the Finnish places where you can spend sats.

name: Fiji
description:
Fiji has a small but growing Bitcoin community, spread across the tourism-driven economy of Viti Levu and Vanua Levu. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Fijian dollar remains the official currency.

The Reserve Bank of Fiji has warned that crypto is not recognised as legal tender and is not regulated, while running a fintech sandbox to study new payment technologies. Adoption remains small and largely peer-to-peer.

Suva and Nadi host occasional meetups and a handful of bitcoin-accepting businesses. Use this map to find the Fijian places where you can spend sats.

name: Falkland Islands
description:
The Falkland Islands, a remote British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic, uses the Falkland Islands pound and has a very small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

British rules apply, and there is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

Stanley hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Falkland Islands places where you can spend sats.

name: Federated States of Micronesia
description:
The Federated States of Micronesia is a Pacific island nation that uses the US dollar and has a very small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

There is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, and adoption remains minimal and peer-to-peer.

Palikir hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Micronesian places where you can spend sats.

name: Faroe Islands
description:
The Faroe Islands, an autonomous territory of Denmark in the North Atlantic, has cheap renewable power and a cold climate. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Danish krone is the currency.

Danish rules apply, and there is no dedicated bitcoin framework; local adoption is minimal, though the islands' energy profile has drawn some mining curiosity.

Tórshavn hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Faroese places where you can spend sats.

name: United Kingdom
description:
The United Kingdom has one of Europe's deepest Bitcoin scenes, with London hosting a long-running community and some of the earliest exchanges, such as Coinfloor, founded in 2013. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

Crypto businesses must register with the FCA for anti-money-laundering purposes, and UK courts have recognised bitcoin as a form of property. Tax-wise, HMRC treats bitcoin as an asset: disposals can attract capital gains tax, while frequent trading may be taxed as income.

From London to Manchester, Bristol and Edinburgh, meetups and bitcoin-accepting merchants keep the scene active. Use this map to find the UK places where you can spend sats.

name: Grenada
description:
Grenada, a small Eastern Caribbean island nation, uses the East Caribbean dollar and has a very small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

The regional central bank has cautioned against crypto, and Grenada has no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

St. George's hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Grenadian places where you can spend sats.

name: Georgia
description:
Georgia has earned a reputation as one of the most Bitcoin-friendly countries, thanks to a liberal tax regime and cheap hydropower that drew miners. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the lari remains the official currency.

Individuals generally pay no tax on bitcoin gains, and crypto trading is exempt from VAT. Since 2023, virtual-asset service providers must register and comply with anti-money-laundering rules overseen by the National Bank of Georgia.

Tbilisi and Batumi host a growing community of meetups and bitcoin-accepting businesses. Use this map to find the Georgian places where you can spend sats.

name: Guernsey
description:
Guernsey, a Crown Dependency and offshore finance centre, has been building rules for crypto businesses, with its financial services commission overseeing virtual-asset providers. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Guernsey pound is used alongside sterling.

A low-tax regime and no capital gains tax support the finance sector, while local Bitcoin adoption remains small and concentrated in Saint Peter Port.

Saint Peter Port hosts a small but international Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Guernsey places where you can spend sats.

name: Ghana
description:
Ghana has become one of West Africa's most active Bitcoin markets, helped by widespread mobile money and a young, mobile-first population. Bitcoin is not legal tender, and the cedi remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned against crypto and barred regulated financial institutions from dealing in it, but authorities have been drafting a regulatory framework, and the securities regulator has issued guidance for digital-asset providers.

Accra and Kumasi host a growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Ghanaian places where you can spend sats.

name: Gibraltar
description:
Gibraltar was one of the first places to regulate crypto, introducing a licensing framework for digital-asset businesses in 2018 under its financial services regulator. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Gibraltar pound is used.

The territory has attracted exchanges and custodians with a clear rulebook and a low-tax regime, including no capital gains tax. Local adoption remains small despite the corporate activity.

Gibraltar hosts a small but international Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Gibraltarian places where you can spend sats.

name: Greenland
description:
Greenland, the vast autonomous territory of Denmark, has drawn interest from Bitcoin miners thanks to abundant hydropower and a cold climate. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Danish krone is the currency.

Danish financial rules apply, and there is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework; local adoption remains minimal, though mining projects have been explored.

Nuuk hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Greenlandic places where you can spend sats.

name: Greece
description:
Bitcoin first drew wide attention in Greece during the financial crisis of the mid-2010s, when capital controls led many to look for alternatives to the banking system. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

Gains on bitcoin are taxed at 15% for individuals, and providers must register with the authorities for anti-money-laundering supervision as EU-wide MiCA rules apply.

Athens and Thessaloniki host meetups and a small but growing set of bitcoin-accepting businesses. Use this map to find the Greek places where you can spend sats.

name: Guatemala
description:
Guatemala has a growing grassroots Bitcoin scene, helped by a huge flow of remittances from the United States and a young population. Bitcoin is not legal tender, and the quetzal remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised, and there is no dedicated licensing regime, so adoption is mostly peer-to-peer and merchant-driven in places such as Antigua.

Guatemala City and Antigua host a small but active Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Guatemalan places where you can spend sats.

name: Hong Kong S.A.R.
description:
Hong Kong, a Special Administrative Region of China, is one of Asia's key Bitcoin hubs, combining a deep financial market with a licensing regime for exchanges introduced in 2023. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Hong Kong dollar remains the official currency.

In 2024 it became the first place in Asia to approve spot bitcoin ETFs, though trading volumes have remained modest. Hong Kong has no capital gains tax, though frequent trading can be taxed as profits.

The city's Bitcoin meetups and a cluster of bitcoin-accepting businesses keep the scene lively. Use this map to find the Hong Kong places where you can spend sats.

name: Croatia
description:
Croatia has a long-running Bitcoin scene, home to Electrocoin, one of the region's oldest bitcoin brokers, and a network of crypto ATMs. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

Providers are supervised under anti-money-laundering rules and, increasingly, EU-wide MiCA, with HANFA as the financial regulator. Gains on bitcoin are taxed as capital income.

Zagreb, Split and Rijeka host meetups and a growing set of bitcoin-accepting businesses. Use this map to find the Croatian places where you can spend sats.

name: Haiti
description:
Haiti has faced prolonged economic and political hardship, and Bitcoin has found a small role for remittances and savings. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the gourde remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned against crypto, and no dedicated licensing framework exists, so adoption remains limited and largely peer-to-peer.

Port-au-Prince hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Haitian places where you can spend sats.

name: Hungary
description:
Hungary has a notable Bitcoin culture: Budapest is home to a bronze statue honouring the pseudonymous creator Satoshi Nakamoto, and the country has an active developer scene. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the forint remains the official currency.

Since 2022 crypto income has been taxed at a flat 15% as separately taxed income, and providers are supervised as EU-wide MiCA rules apply.

Budapest hosts regular meetups and a growing set of bitcoin-accepting businesses. Use this map to find the Hungarian places where you can spend sats.

name: Indonesia
description:
Indonesia is one of the world's most active Bitcoin markets, with a huge young population and millions of retail users. Bitcoin is legal to buy and hold, but the central bank prohibits using it as a means of payment.

Crypto assets are treated as commodities: the market was long overseen by Bappebti and, since 2025, supervision has shifted to the OJK. Transactions on registered exchanges carry a 0.1% final income tax plus VAT, making the tax bite small but ever-present.

From Jakarta to Bali and Surabaya, meetups and a growing set of bitcoin-accepting venues keep the scene thriving. Use this map to find the Indonesian places where you can spend sats.

name: Ireland
description:
Ireland has a compact but active Bitcoin scene, centred on Dublin and its large tech sector. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

Tax is steep: gains are charged at the 33% capital gains rate, and bitcoin received as payment or income is taxed at income-tax rates. The Central Bank of Ireland requires service providers to register for anti-money-laundering supervision.

From Dublin to Cork and Galway, meetups and bitcoin-accepting businesses keep the community connected. Use this map to find the Irish places where you can spend sats.

name: Israel
description:
Israel has a deep Bitcoin culture: Tel Aviv's Bitcoin Embassy, founded in 2013, is one of the oldest community hubs of its kind. Bitcoin is legal but not legal tender, and the shekel remains the only official currency.

For tax, the Israel Tax Authority treats bitcoin as an asset rather than currency, so individuals generally pay a 25% capital gains tax, plus a surtax for high earners. Regulators have pushed banks to serve bitcoin customers instead of turning them away outright.

From Tel Aviv to Jerusalem and Haifa, meetups and bitcoin-accepting merchants keep the community lively. Use this map to find the Israeli places where you can spend sats.

name: Isle of Man
description:
The Isle of Man has long courted digital-asset businesses, requiring crypto firms to register with its financial services authority under anti-money-laundering rules. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Manx pound is used alongside sterling.

A low-tax regime and a clear rulebook have attracted exchanges and service providers, though local adoption remains modest. There is no capital gains tax.

Douglas hosts a small but international Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Manx places where you can spend sats.

name: India
description:
India is home to one of the world's largest grassroots bitcoin markets, spanning a huge developer base and millions of retail users. Bitcoin is legal but not legal tender; the rupee remains the only official currency, and the Supreme Court struck down an earlier banking ban in 2020.

Taxation is heavy: since 2022 gains are taxed at a flat 30% with no loss offset, and a 1% tax is withheld on every transfer. In 2023 virtual-asset businesses were brought under anti-money-laundering rules and required to register with the FIU, while the RBI continues to urge caution.

From Bengaluru and Mumbai to Delhi, meetups, developers and a growing set of merchants keep the scene moving. Use this map to find the Indian places where you can spend sats.

name: Iraq
description:
Iraq has seen growing interest in Bitcoin as a way to move money and protect savings amid a volatile dinar and a large informal dollar market. Bitcoin is not legal tender, and the central bank has warned against crypto.

There is no licensing framework for bitcoin businesses, and authorities have occasionally moved against unlicensed platforms, so activity is largely peer-to-peer.

Baghdad and Erbil host small Bitcoin communities. Use this map to find the Iraqi places where you can spend sats.

name: Iceland
description:
Iceland's cheap geothermal and hydroelectric power made it an unlikely early home for Bitcoin mining, and its 2008 banking collapse gave Icelanders a keen interest in alternatives to traditional finance. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the króna remains the official currency.

Capital gains on bitcoin are taxed at 22%, and authorities have discussed the strain mining can place on the grid. Service providers are subject to anti-money-laundering rules.

Reykjavik's meetups and a scattering of bitcoin-accepting businesses keep the scene alive. Use this map to find the Icelandic places where you can spend sats.

name: Italy
description:
Italy is one of Europe's largest Bitcoin economies, with a growing merchant scene and a community that stretches from Milan and Turin to Rome and Naples. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

Since 2022, providers have had to register on a dedicated list run by the OAM, and the Bank of Italy and Consob now supervise them as EU-wide MiCA rules apply. Gains on bitcoin have been taxed at 26% since 2023, though higher rates have been proposed in parliament.

Meetups and bitcoin-accepting shops are spreading across Italian cities and towns. Use this map to find the Italian places where you can spend sats.

name: Jersey
description:
Jersey, a Crown Dependency and offshore finance centre, requires virtual-currency businesses to register with its financial regulator for anti-money-laundering purposes. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Jersey pound is used alongside sterling.

A low-tax regime with no capital gains tax has made the island attractive to fund managers and crypto firms, while local adoption remains small.

Saint Helier hosts a small but international Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Jersey places where you can spend sats.

name: Jamaica
description:
Jamaica has one of the Caribbean's more active crypto scenes, and in 2022 it became one of the first countries to launch a national digital currency, JAM-DEX. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Jamaican dollar remains the official currency.

The Bank of Jamaica has warned against crypto and focused on its own digital dollar, leaving bitcoin largely unregulated and used mainly for remittances and small payments.

Kingston hosts a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Jamaican places where you can spend sats.

name: Jordan
description:
Jordan has a young, tech-literate population and a growing interest in Bitcoin, though the central bank has not recognised it as legal tender. The dinar remains the official currency.

The Central Bank of Jordan has warned against crypto, and no dedicated licensing regime exists, so trading is mostly peer-to-peer and through offshore platforms. Officials have studied digital currencies but remain cautious.

Amman hosts a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Jordanian places where you can spend sats.

name: Japan
description:
The pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin, Satoshi Nakamoto, chose a Japanese name, and Japan has been central to the currency's story ever since. Tokyo was home to Mt. Gox, the world's largest bitcoin exchange until its collapse in 2014, which at its peak handled roughly 70% of all global trades.

In April 2017 Japan became one of the first major economies to formally recognize bitcoin as a legal method of payment under its amended Payment Services Act, with exchanges supervised by the Financial Services Agency. Large retailers began accepting BTC around the same time, and bitcoin is treated as property and taxed as miscellaneous income.

Today a lively community keeps the ecosystem alive through meetups in Tokyo, Osaka and beyond, while exchanges and merchants continue to serve an active market in a country with a deep trading history. Use this map to find the places where you can spend sats across Japan.

name: Kenya
description:
Kenya has one of the world's most advanced mobile-money cultures, thanks to M-Pesa, and that payments-first mindset has carried over to bitcoin. Bitcoin is legal but not legal tender, and the Central Bank has repeatedly cautioned against it rather than banned it.

Regulation is taking shape: the Finance Act 2023 introduced a 3% tax on digital-asset transfers, and authorities have been drafting a framework to license service providers. Kenya has also become a quiet leader in bitcoin mining, with projects such as Gridless powering miners from off-grid hydro and other renewable plants.

Nairobi's meetups and a growing number of bitcoin-accepting merchants keep the community active. Use this map to find the Kenyan places where you can spend sats.

name: Kyrgyzstan
description:
Kyrgyzstan has taken a relatively open approach to Bitcoin, passing a Virtual Assets Law in 2022 that established licensing for exchanges and providers. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the som remains the official currency.

The financial regulator oversees licensed platforms, and cheap hydropower has made the country attractive for mining. Adoption remains small and concentrated around Bishkek.

Bishkek hosts a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Kyrgyz places where you can spend sats.

name: Kiribati
description:
Kiribati is a vast, low-lying Pacific island nation that uses the Australian dollar and faces severe climate risk. Bitcoin remains a very small niche.

There is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, and adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

South Tarawa hosts a negligible Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the I-Kiribati places where you can spend sats.

name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
description:
Saint Kitts and Nevis is a small twin-island nation and offshore-finance centre where Bitcoin remains a niche interest. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the East Caribbean dollar is the official currency.

Regulators have cautioned against crypto and no dedicated licensing framework exists, though the government has expressed interest in digital-asset innovation. Local adoption is minimal.

Basseterre hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Kittitian places where you can spend sats.

name: South Korea
description:
South Korea has one of the world's largest retail Bitcoin markets, famous for the 'Kimchi premium' when local prices run above global ones. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the won remains the official currency.

Regulation is strict: since 2021 exchanges must register with the financial authorities and secure real-name bank accounts, a rule that wiped out many smaller platforms. A Virtual Asset User Protection Act took effect in 2024, and plans to tax bitcoin gains have been repeatedly postponed.

Seoul and Busan host active meetups and a dense trading culture that keeps Korea central to Asia's Bitcoin scene. Use this map to find the South Korean places where you can spend sats.

name: Kuwait
description:
Kuwait has kept Bitcoin at arm's length: the central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised, and regulators have barred licensed financial firms from dealing in virtual assets. The Kuwaiti dinar is the only legal tender.

There is no licensing path for bitcoin businesses, so activity is limited and informal, though interest persists among a young population. Officials have explored digital-currency projects of their own.

Kuwait City hosts a small, low-key Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Kuwaiti places where you can spend sats.

name: Cayman Islands
description:
The Cayman Islands is one of the world's largest offshore financial centres and a major domicile for crypto investment funds. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Cayman Islands dollar is pegged to the US dollar.

In 2020 the territory passed the Virtual Asset (Service Providers) Act, bringing custodians and exchanges under the Cayman Islands Monetary Authority. There is no income or capital gains tax.

George Town hosts a small but international Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Caymanian places where you can spend sats.

name: Kazakhstan
description:
Kazakhstan became a Bitcoin-mining heavyweight after China's 2021 crackdown, thanks to cheap coal power that briefly pushed it into the global top three for hashrate. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the tenge remains the official currency.

Mining brought power shortages and a regulatory response: officials required miners to register, limited electricity use and clamped down on unlicensed operations, while a Digital Assets Law and the AIFC created a licensing path for exchanges. Using bitcoin as a means of payment is not allowed.

Almaty and Astana host mining operations and a growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Kazakh places where you can spend sats.

name: Lebanon
description:
Lebanon's banking crisis, which erupted in 2019, pushed many people toward Bitcoin as the lira collapsed and dollar withdrawals were frozen. Bitcoin is not legal tender, and there is no dedicated licensing framework.

The central bank has warned against crypto and does not recognise it, but enforcement has been limited, and peer-to-peer trading grew as a way to receive remittances and protect savings.

Beirut hosts a small but determined Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Lebanese places where you can spend sats.

name: Saint Lucia
description:
Saint Lucia, an Eastern Caribbean island nation, uses the East Caribbean dollar and belongs to a currency union that has piloted a regional digital currency. Bitcoin remains a small niche.

The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank has cautioned against crypto, and Saint Lucia has no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

Castries hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Saint Lucian places where you can spend sats.

name: Liechtenstein
description:
Liechtenstein was an early mover on digital-asset law, passing its Token and Virtual-Asset Service Providers Act in 2020 and creating one of the first comprehensive frameworks of its kind. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Swiss franc is the currency.

The Financial Market Authority supervises providers, and the country has attracted token-focused businesses. For private individuals, capital gains on bitcoin are generally not taxed, though a wealth tax applies.

Vaduz hosts a small but international Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Liechtenstein places where you can spend sats.

name: Sri Lanka
description:
Sri Lanka's economic crisis of 2022 pushed many people toward Bitcoin as the rupee and the banking system came under strain. Bitcoin is not legal tender, and the Sri Lankan rupee remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised and carries risk, while the government has studied a framework to regulate digital assets and their taxation. Adoption remains grassroots and largely peer-to-peer.

Colombo's meetups keep a small but engaged Bitcoin community going. Use this map to find the Sri Lankan places where you can spend sats.

name: Lesotho
description:
Lesotho has a small and mostly informal Bitcoin scene, shaped by remittances from South Africa and high mobile-money use. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the loti remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised or regulated, and no licensing framework exists, so adoption remains limited and peer-to-peer.

Maseru hosts a small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Lesotho places where you can spend sats.

name: Lithuania
description:
Lithuania has become a fintech gateway in the Baltics and, for a time, one of Europe's easiest places to register a crypto business. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

Service providers have had to register with the financial-crime watchdog since 2020, and supervision has shifted to the Bank of Lithuania under EU-wide MiCA. Gains on bitcoin are taxed at 15%.

Vilnius hosts meetups and a small but active community. Use this map to find the Lithuanian places where you can spend sats.

name: Luxembourg
description:
Luxembourg is one of Europe's financial hubs and a base for cross-border Bitcoin businesses, including the exchange Bitstamp, which secured an EU payment licence here in 2016. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

The financial regulator, the CSSF, oversees providers as part of the EU's MiCA framework. For private investors, Luxembourg is generally friendly: there is no broad capital gains tax on bitcoin held longer than six months.

Luxembourg City's meetups keep a small but international community connected. Use this map to find the Luxembourg places where you can spend sats.

name: Latvia
description:
Latvia has a modest but growing Bitcoin community centred on Riga, with a fintech sector that has expanded steadily. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

Service providers must register with the tax authority for anti-money-laundering purposes, and oversight is passing to the central bank under EU-wide MiCA. Gains on bitcoin are taxed at 20% as capital income.

Riga's meetups keep the local scene connected. Use this map to find the Latvian places where you can spend sats.

name: Morocco
description:
Morocco has one of Africa's highest rates of grassroots Bitcoin use, even though the authorities declared crypto transactions illegal back in 2017. Bitcoin is not legal tender, and the dirham remains the official currency.

Officials have warned that using virtual assets breaches exchange and anti-money-laundering rules, but enforcement has been light and peer-to-peer trading continues. In 2024 the central bank began preparing a law to regulate crypto assets, signalling a shift from prohibition toward oversight.

Casablanca and Marrakech host a quiet but persistent Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Moroccan places where you can spend sats.

name: Saint Martin
description:
Saint Martin is the French overseas collectivity on the northern half of a Caribbean island it shares with Sint Maarten. It uses the euro and has a very small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

French and EU rules apply, and there is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

Marigot hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the places where you can spend sats.

name: Madagascar
description:
Madagascar has a young population and a growing mobile-money market, and Bitcoin has begun to attract attention as a savings and remittance option. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the ariary remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised or regulated, and no licensing framework exists, so adoption remains small and peer-to-peer.

Antananarivo hosts a small but curious Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Malagasy places where you can spend sats.

name: Marshall Islands
description:
The Marshall Islands, a small Pacific nation that uses the US dollar, has taken an unusual path: it planned its own national digital currency, the Sovereign, though the project has not launched amid international concerns. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

In 2022 the country amended its company law to recognise decentralised autonomous organisations, one of the first to do so. Local Bitcoin adoption remains minimal.

Majuro hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Marshallese places where you can spend sats.

name: Mongolia
description:
Mongolia has become an unexpected home for Bitcoin mining, drawn by cheap coal-fired power and cold winters that help keep rigs cool. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the tögrög remains the official currency.

The boom has been bumpy: authorities cracked down on illegal mining connections and restricted power use during shortages, and the central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised as legal tender. Regulation is still taking shape.

Ulaanbaatar hosts a small but persistent Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Mongolian places where you can spend sats.

name: Montserrat
description:
Montserrat, a small British Overseas Territory in the Caribbean, uses the East Caribbean dollar and has a very small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

The regional central bank has cautioned against crypto, and there is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

Brades hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Montserrat places where you can spend sats.

name: Malta
description:
Malta has long courted digital-asset businesses, and in 2018 it passed one of the EU's first licensing regimes for crypto service providers, supervised by the MFSA. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the euro remains the official currency.

The island attracted major exchanges and, under EU-wide MiCA, has continued to license providers. For individuals, Malta generally does not tax capital gains on bitcoin, though regular trading can be treated as income.

Valletta and Sliema host meetups and a small but international Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Maltese places where you can spend sats.

name: Mauritius
description:
Mauritius has positioned itself as a fintech bridge between Africa and Asia, and in 2021 it passed the Virtual Asset and Initial Token Offering Services Act, one of the continent's first dedicated licensing regimes. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Mauritian rupee remains the official currency.

The Financial Services Commission supervises licensed providers, and the framework was tightened as the country worked to satisfy global anti-money-laundering standards. Adoption remains small and institutional-leaning.

Port Louis hosts a small but international Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Mauritian places where you can spend sats.

name: Maldives
description:
The Maldives is a tourism-driven economy with a growing interest in fintech, and Bitcoin remains a niche curiosity. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the rufiyaa remains the official currency.

The Maldives Monetary Authority has warned that crypto is not recognised or regulated, and no licensing framework exists, so adoption remains minimal and peer-to-peer.

Malé hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Maldivian places where you can spend sats.

name: Mexico
description:
Mexico is one of the largest remittance markets in the world, receiving tens of billions of dollars a year, which has made bitcoin an appealing alternative for cheaper cross-border transfers. Bitcoin is legal here, though not legal tender, and the peso remains the only official currency.

The country's 2018 Fintech Law was among the first in the region to regulate virtual assets, but central-bank rules have largely kept banks from offering bitcoin directly, so adoption runs through non-bank exchanges and peer-to-peer trading.

From Mexico City to Guadalajara and Monterrey, meetups and bitcoin-accepting merchants keep the scene growing. Use this map to find the Mexican places where you can spend sats.

name: Malaysia
description:
Malaysia has a well-defined approach to Bitcoin, with digital-asset exchanges required to register with the Securities Commission and a Shariah ruling that permits trading on approved platforms. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the ringgit remains the official currency.

Malaysia has no broad capital gains tax, though frequent trading can be taxed as income. The regulator has generally encouraged blockchain activity while warning against unlicensed platforms.

Kuala Lumpur and Penang host meetups and a modest set of bitcoin-accepting businesses. Use this map to find the Malaysian places where you can spend sats.

name: Mozambique
description:
Mozambique has a growing mobile-money culture and a young population, and Bitcoin has started to find a niche for remittances and savings. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the metical remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised as legal tender and no dedicated licensing regime exists, so activity remains informal and peer-to-peer.

Maputo hosts a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Mozambican places where you can spend sats.

name: Namibia
description:
Namibia moved from caution to regulation, passing a Virtual Assets Act in 2023 that licenses service providers and aligns with global anti-money-laundering standards. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Namibian dollar remains the official currency.

The central bank had long warned that crypto was not legal tender, and the new law created an oversight framework shared by the Bank of Namibia and NAMFISA. Adoption remains small and mostly peer-to-peer.

Windhoek hosts a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Namibian places where you can spend sats.

name: New Caledonia
description:
New Caledonia, a French special collectivity in the South Pacific, is a major nickel producer with a small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the CFP franc is the currency.

French and EU-aligned rules apply, and there is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption remains minimal and peer-to-peer.

Nouméa hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Caledonian places where you can spend sats.

name: Nigeria
description:
Nigeria is one of the world's largest grassroots Bitcoin markets, driven by a fast-depreciating naira, high inflation and a young, mobile-first population looking for a reliable store of value and cheaper remittances.

The regulatory path has been volatile: in 2021 the Central Bank barred banks from serving bitcoin businesses, then reversed course in late 2023 and issued guidelines allowing them back in, while the SEC began licensing digital-asset exchanges. Bitcoin is not legal tender, but peer-to-peer trading here ranks among the busiest on the planet.

Communities in Lagos, Abuja and beyond keep the scene vibrant with meetups and education, and merchants from cafes to tech shops increasingly accept sats. Use this map to find the places where you can spend bitcoin across Nigeria.

name: Netherlands
description:
The Netherlands has been a European Bitcoin pioneer for over a decade. Amsterdam is home to Bitonic, one of the continent's oldest bitcoin brokers, and hosts Bitcoin Amsterdam, one of Europe's largest Bitcoin-only conferences.

The city of Arnhem is a standout: local shops along the Koningstraat—informally the Bitcoin Boulevard—accept bitcoin, part of a long-running effort to build a circular bitcoin economy. Regulation is clear, with service providers registering with the Dutch central bank.

Taxwise there is no separate capital gains tax on bitcoin; instead holdings form part of the wealth-tax base in Box 3. From Amsterdam to Arnhem and beyond, meetups and merchants keep the scene thriving. Use this map to find the Dutch places where you can spend sats.

name: Nepal
description:
Nepal has become an unlikely hotspot for Bitcoin interest, driven by remittances and a young population—despite a 2017 ban from the central bank that made virtual-currency trading illegal. The Nepalese rupee is the only legal tender.

Enforcement has been real, with arrests and seizures reported, yet peer-to-peer activity and curiosity persist. The central bank has studied the technology and periodically signalled that a regulatory framework may be needed.

Kathmandu and Pokhara host a small, cautious Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Nepali places where you can spend sats.

name: Nauru
description:
Nauru is a tiny Pacific island nation that uses the Australian dollar and has a very small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

There is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, and adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

Yaren hosts a negligible Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Nauruan places where you can spend sats.

name: New Zealand
description:
New Zealand is a small country with an outsized Bitcoin community, with meetups in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the New Zealand dollar remains the official currency.

The tax picture is nuanced: New Zealand has no general capital gains tax, but if you acquire bitcoin for the purpose of disposal, gains can be taxed as income. Authorities have been cautious, and the Reserve Bank is also exploring a digital version of the dollar.

From city cafes to coastal towns, bitcoin-accepting merchants and events keep the scene friendly and growing. Use this map to find the New Zealand places where you can spend sats.

name: Oman
description:
Oman moved to regulate crypto in 2023, when its Capital Market Authority issued a virtual-assets framework covering exchanges, brokers and custodians. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Omani rial remains the official currency.

The rules aim to attract licensed firms while meeting anti-money-laundering standards, and there is no personal income tax. Adoption remains early and concentrated around Muscat.

Muscat hosts a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Omani places where you can spend sats.

name: Panama
description:
Panama briefly looked set to embrace crypto, but a 2022 law regulating virtual assets was partially vetoed over anti-money-laundering concerns, leaving the sector largely in limbo. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender; the US dollar circulates alongside the balboa.

With no central bank and a dollar-based economy, Panama is an attractive base for international business, while the government weighs how to regulate digital assets without running afoul of global AML standards.

Panama City's Bitcoin meetups and a small set of accepting businesses keep the scene present. Use this map to find the Panamanian places where you can spend sats.

name: Peru
description:
Peru has become one of Latin America's more active Bitcoin markets, helped by a large informal economy, remittances and a young population. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the sol remains the official currency.

Regulators have moved to bring crypto providers under anti-money-laundering rules, though comprehensive legislation is still pending. Gains are generally taxable as income under existing rules.

Lima's meetups and a growing set of merchants keep the scene moving, with interest spreading to Arequipa and Trujillo. Use this map to find the Peruvian places where you can spend sats.

name: French Polynesia
description:
French Polynesia, a French overseas collectivity spread across the South Pacific, has a tourism-driven economy and a small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the CFP franc is the currency.

French and EU-aligned rules apply, and there is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption remains minimal and concentrated among a few enthusiasts.

Papeete hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Polynesian places where you can spend sats.

name: Papua New Guinea
description:
Papua New Guinea has a small and largely informal Bitcoin scene, with interest driven by remittances and a young population. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the kina remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised or regulated, and no licensing framework exists, so adoption remains limited and peer-to-peer.

Port Moresby hosts a small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Papua New Guinean places where you can spend sats.

name: Philippines
description:
The Philippines is one of the world's fastest-growing Bitcoin markets, driven by a huge remittance economy and a young, mobile-first population. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the peso remains the official currency.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has regulated virtual-asset service providers since 2017, requiring them to register, and local firms such as Pouch are building remittances and payroll on top of the Lightning Network.

From Manila to Cebu and Davao, meetups and a growing set of merchants keep the scene active. Use this map to find the Filipino places where you can spend sats.

name: Pakistan
description:
Pakistan is one of the world's fastest-growing Bitcoin markets, driven by inflation, remittances and a young, mobile-first population. Bitcoin is not legal tender, and the rupee remains the official currency.

Regulation has whipsawed: banks were barred from crypto in 2018, and after years of ambiguity the government created a dedicated virtual-assets authority and a crypto council in 2025, signalling a shift toward licensing and even strategic mining plans.

Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad host active Bitcoin communities. Use this map to find the Pakistani places where you can spend sats.

name: Poland
description:
Poland has one of Europe's largest networks of bitcoin ATMs and a fast-growing merchant scene, particularly in its bigger cities. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the złoty remains the official currency.

Providers must register for anti-money-laundering purposes with the tax administration, and gains on bitcoin are taxed at a flat 19%. The country also has a large and vocal Bitcoin community, with regular meetups in Warsaw, Kraków and Wrocław.

From the Baltic coast to the Tatra mountains, bitcoin-accepting businesses are spreading. Use this map to find the Polish places where you can spend sats.

name: Saint Pierre and Miquelon
description:
Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a French archipelago off the coast of Newfoundland, uses the euro and has a very small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

French and EU rules apply, and there is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

Saint-Pierre hosts a negligible Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the places where you can spend sats.

name: Puerto Rico
description:
Puerto Rico is a US territory where federal rules apply, and its generous tax incentives have drawn a wave of crypto entrepreneurs and investors. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the US dollar is the currency.

Because it follows US tax law, bitcoin is treated as property and taxed accordingly, and local authorities have moved cautiously on licensing. Adoption is uneven, with pockets of activity in San Juan.

San Juan hosts a small but active Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Puerto Rican places where you can spend sats.

name: Portugal
description:
Portugal has long been a favourite base for Bitcoiners, thanks to a mild climate, a growing tech scene and a tax regime that for years left individual bitcoin gains untaxed. Bitcoin is not legal tender here, but it is fully legal to buy, hold and spend.

In 2023 the rules changed: gains on bitcoin held for less than a year are now taxed at 28%, while longer-term holdings remain exempt. The autonomous region of Madeira has gone further, promoting a free-trade zone with generous tax treatment and courting Bitcoin businesses and events.

Lisbon and Porto host a dense calendar of meetups and conferences, and bitcoin-accepting merchants can be found in cities across the country. Use this map to find the Portuguese places where you can spend sats.

name: Palau
description:
Palau, a small Pacific island nation that uses the US dollar, has experimented with a national digital currency pilot in partnership with a fintech firm. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

There is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, and adoption remains minimal, though the government has shown openness to digital-asset technology.

Ngerulmud and Koror host a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Palauan places where you can spend sats.

name: Qatar
description:
Qatar has taken a cautious line on Bitcoin: in 2020 the Qatar Financial Centre banned regulated firms from dealing in virtual assets, and the central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised. The riyal is the only legal tender.

Interest has grown quietly anyway, and in 2024 the central bank began work on a digital version of the riyal. There is no licensing regime for bitcoin businesses, so activity remains informal.

Doha hosts a small, low-key Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Qatari places where you can spend sats.

name: Romania
description:
Romania has one of Eastern Europe's larger Bitcoin communities, powered by a strong IT workforce and a network of meetups in Bucharest, Cluj and Timișoara. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the leu remains the official currency.

Crypto providers must be authorised under anti-money-laundering rules that predate EU-wide MiCA, and the tax authority taxes gains as income. The country has also seen debate over how heavily to tax digital-asset gains.

Bucharest and Cluj host regular meetups and a growing set of bitcoin-accepting merchants. Use this map to find the Romanian places where you can spend sats.

name: Republic of Serbia
description:
Serbia was one of the first countries in the region to adopt a dedicated digital-assets law, in 2020, putting bitcoin on a formal legal footing. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the dinar remains the official currency.

The National Bank of Serbia supervises exchange and custody services, and capital gains on bitcoin are taxed at 15%. The framework has helped make Belgrade a base for local Bitcoin businesses.

Belgrade, Novi Sad and Niš host meetups and a growing set of bitcoin-accepting businesses. Use this map to find the Serbian places where you can spend sats.

name: Rwanda
description:
Rwanda's tech-forward government has made it one of East Africa's more digitally advanced countries, and Bitcoin has quietly followed. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Rwandan franc remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised or regulated, while the capital-market regulator has been building a framework and sandbox to supervise digital assets. Adoption remains small and peer-to-peer.

Kigali hosts a small but growing Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Rwandan places where you can spend sats.

name: Saudi Arabia
description:
Saudi Arabia has taken a cautious line on Bitcoin: in 2018 the central bank and the capital-market regulator warned that trading in virtual currencies was illegal and barred banks from processing crypto transactions. The riyal, pegged to the US dollar, is the only legal tender.

Interest in digital assets has grown anyway, and the kingdom has explored blockchain and central-bank digital currency projects alongside the UAE. More recently, officials have signalled they are studying how to regulate digital assets rather than ignore them.

Riyadh and Jeddah host a small, low-key Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Saudi places where you can spend sats.

name: Solomon Islands
description:
The Solomon Islands is a small, aid- and remittance-dependent Pacific economy, and Bitcoin remains a niche interest. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Solomon Islands dollar remains the official currency.

The central bank has warned that crypto is not recognised or regulated, and no licensing framework exists, so activity is minimal and peer-to-peer.

Honiara hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Solomon Islands places where you can spend sats.

name: Sweden
description:
Sweden is one of the world's most cashless societies and a pioneer in central-bank digital-currency research, yet it also has a small but determined Bitcoin community. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the krona remains the official currency.

Gains on bitcoin are taxed at 30% as capital income, with losses partly deductible. Mining has grown in the north thanks to cheap hydro and wind power, though tax authorities have scrutinized its energy use.

Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö host meetups and a modest set of bitcoin-accepting businesses. Use this map to find the Swedish places where you can spend sats.

name: Singapore
description:
Singapore is one of Asia's main financial hubs and a popular base for Bitcoin companies. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore licenses digital payment token providers under its Payment Services Act.

The tax regime is famously light: there is no capital gains tax, and bitcoin is exempt from GST, though frequent trading can be taxed as income. Since 2022 authorities have restricted public crypto advertising and removed bitcoin ATMs to protect retail investors.

A tight-knit community of developers, meetups and merchants keeps the scene active across the island. Use this map to find the Singaporean places where you can spend sats.

name: Saint Helena
description:
Saint Helena, a remote British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic, uses the Saint Helena pound and has a very small Bitcoin following. Bitcoin is legal, but not legal tender.

British rules apply, and there is no dedicated bitcoin licensing framework, so adoption is minimal and peer-to-peer.

Jamestown hosts a very small Bitcoin community. Use this map to find the Saint Helena places where you can spend sats.

name: Slovenia
description:
